title: Why catching a rocket matters - and what it does not prove
dek: SpaceX's tower caught a Starship returning from orbit. To see why that is a big deal, start with an aeroplane ticket.

article: When SpaceX's giant tower arms closed around a returning Starship on 14 November, the company celebrated a first. But what does the milestone actually mean - and what does it not mean?

To understand why a catch matters, think about air travel. Imagine if every passenger jet were scrapped after a single flight: tickets would be unaffordable. For most of the space age, rockets worked exactly like that, and each launch threw away hardware worth tens of millions of dollars.

SpaceX began to change this about a decade ago by landing and reusing the first stage of its Falcon 9 rocket. Analysts estimate this helped bring the cost of putting a kilogram into orbit down to roughly $2,700, compared with $10,000 or more in the era of throwaway rockets. Yet Falcon 9's upper stage is still discarded on every flight.

Starship is designed to go further: both of its stages are meant to return and fly again quickly. If that works, supporters believe launch costs could fall to somewhere between $10 and $50 a kilogram. Catching the upper stage, which faces the fiercest heat as it plunges back through the atmosphere, is an essential step towards that goal.

Cheaper, more frequent launches would ripple outwards. Starship can carry far more of SpaceX's newest Starlink internet satellites, each of which handles about ten times the traffic of the previous model. Elon Musk has said SpaceX will retire Falcon 9 once Starship flies reliably every week.

The milestone also matters for the Moon. NASA plans to use a version of Starship to land astronauts there, but the lander must be refuelled in orbit, by some estimates with around ten tanker flights. That plan only makes sense if launches become routine and affordable.

Nevertheless, caution is warranted. The $10-to-$50 figure is a target, not an established price, and some analysts point out that Musk's numbers describe SpaceX's own costs rather than what customers will pay. On the same flight, the booster was lost, and no Ship has yet been inspected, refuelled and relaunched quickly - the real test of reuse.
In short, the catch shows that the hardest piece of the puzzle can come home intact. Whether it can turn into cheap, airline-style spaceflight is a question the next few years will answer.

too expensive for people to pay for

SpaceX's newest Starlink satellites carry ten times more traffic
tasks.explain: A matches the question in paragraph 1 and the answer in paragraph 8. B is an overclaim (paragraph 7 says the costs are only targets). C twists paragraph 5: Falcon 9 retires only once Starship flies weekly. D is one detail from paragraph 5.

write.prompt: Do you think reusable rockets will make space travel common in your lifetime? Write 2-3 sentences in English, using one word from today's list.
write.sample: I think reusable rockets could make space travel more routine, but I am not sure it will happen soon. The catch was an important milestone, yet caution is warranted until a Ship actually flies again.

title_zh: 接住火箭為什麼重要——以及它還證明不了什麼
dek_zh: SpaceX 的發射塔接住了一艘從軌道返回的星艦。要理解這有多重要，先從一張機票說起。
article_zh: 11 月 14 日，SpaceX 巨大的發射塔機械臂夾住了一艘返回的星艦（Starship），公司慶祝了這項首次成就。但這個里程碑實際上代表什麼——又不代表什麼？
要理解「接住」為什麼重要，想想搭飛機。想像每架客機飛一趟就報廢：機票會貴到買不起。在太空時代的大部分時間裡，火箭正是這樣運作的，每次發射都丟掉價值數千萬美元的硬體。
大約十年前，SpaceX 開始透過回收並重複使用獵鷹九號（Falcon 9）的第一節來改變這一點。分析師估計，這幫助把送一公斤進入軌道的成本降到大約 2,700 美元，而在用完即丟的火箭時代要 1 萬美元以上。不過，獵鷹九號的上節每次飛行仍會被丟棄。
星艦的設計目標更進一步：兩節都要能返回並快速再次飛行。如果成功，支持者相信發射成本可能降到每公斤 10 到 50 美元之間。接住上節——它在衝回大氣層時承受最猛烈的高溫——是邁向這個目標不可或缺的一步。
更便宜、更頻繁的發射會產生連鎖效應。星艦能載運更多 SpaceX 最新的星鏈（Starlink）網路衛星，每顆的流量約是上一代的十倍。馬斯克曾表示，一旦星艦能可靠地每週飛行，SpaceX 就會讓獵鷹九號退役。
這個里程碑對登月也很重要。NASA 計畫用一款星艦把太空人送上月球，但這艘登陸艇必須在軌道上加油，有估計認為需要大約十趟加油船飛行。只有在發射變得例行且負擔得起時，這個計畫才說得通。
儘管如此，仍應保持謹慎。每公斤 10 到 50 美元是目標，不是既定價格；一些分析師也指出，馬斯克的數字描述的是 SpaceX 自己的成本，而不是客戶要付的價錢。在同一次飛行中，助推器損毀了；而且還沒有任何一艘星艦經過檢查、加油並迅速再次發射——那才是重複使用的真正考驗。
簡而言之，這次接住顯示：拼圖中最難的那一塊可以完好無缺地回家。至於它能否變成便宜、像航空公司一樣的太空飛行，要由接下來幾年來回答。
